docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
Welcome! This is a mini role-playing adventure game featuring raccoons drinking beer and racing stolen cars. Do I need to say anything more?

Perhaps a little more…

Players take on the role of trash pandas (i.e., raccoons) who do distinctly human-like things. A Raccoon Wrangler (RW) runs the game, makes rulings, and plays the city and the occasional animals, people, and race car drivers the player raccoons might encounter.

This game is improvisational, with only a few rules and mechanics. You need a handful of six-sided dice, an RW, two or more players, some pencils, and the character sheet in Appendix B.

This document has two parts: the first explains the basics for players, and the second offers advice for the RW.

The idea for this game came about after an evening in the Texas piney woods with a precocious raccoon fascinated by our barbecue grill. I’m sure he’s still out there, grilling his dinners and knocking back a beer as I type.

Enjoy!

Zachary Taylor April 2023

docs.title: Disclaimer
docs.text: This is a game. It in no way condones raccoons operating heavy machinery while under the influence. No raccoons were harmed in the making of this game, though several beers disappeared.

docs.title: Appendix A: Raccoon-Approved Cocktail Recipes
docs.text: Each of the following cocktails removes two points of stress. Your RW might like one, too.

docs.title: Salty Raccoon
docs.text:
• 1.5 oz tequila
  • 1 oz rosemary simple syrup (see following recipe)
  • 1 oz fresh lime juice
  • sea salt
  • a charred sprig of rosemary

Line half the rim of a glass with sea salt. Add ice and set aside. Shake all ingredients with ice in a shaker, then strain into the ice-filled glass. Char a sprig of rosemary and use it as a garnish. Or eat it — you’re a raccoon.

docs.title: Rosemary Simple Syrup
docs.text:
• 2 cups sugar
  • 1 cup water
  • 4–5 sprigs of fresh rosemary

Bring the water to a boil. Add sugar and stir until dissolved. Remove from heat. Add rosemary and let cool. Strain. Refrigerate in a covered container for up to a week.

docs.title: Raccoon's Revenge
docs.text:
• 1.5 oz coffee liqueur
  • 4.5 oz Dr. Pepper
  • 3 oz vodka

Mix and serve over 6 ice cubes (not 7, not 5… 6). Fun fact: Raccoons can't count.

docs.title: Trashed Crash Pandas?
docs.text:
Yes. You're a (mostly) normal but (decidedly) uncommon raccoon who drinks beer and drives race cars. You can't read or speak human language, but you can communicate with other animals. What sets you apart from others of your kind is your heightened ambition. Other trash pandas may want things (mainly trash) or know things (mainly where to find trash), but for the most part, they're not up for grocery shopping, evading law enforcement, or driving an 18-wheeler on the interstate.

You might be dismissed as a “common raccoon” (Procyon lotor to friends), but you ain’t common. Sure, you occasionally indulge in people’s trash — that goes without saying. But you’re no one’s pet!

docs.title: Raccoon Racer
docs.text:
Why are you, a raccoon, entering the world of illegal street racing and looking for beer? Are you in this for love, fortune, fame, or justice? Who’s your rival? Are they human? Do they even know you exist? What burning conflict in your beating procyonine heart spurs the drama?

Name your raccoon and write a sentence or two describing them, their backstory, or their motivations. A printable character sheet is included in Appendix B.

docs.title: The Smack’s Talents
docs.text:
Each raccoon brings one exceptional talent to your smack. Smack? It's the collective noun for raccoons.

Choose one talent from the list below for your raccoon. This talent is a specific skill your raccoon excels at.

Note: Each talent can be chosen only once, so every raccoon in the smack will have a unique talent.

Talent What It Means Brains Helping another raccoon Face Duping humans Fingers Using human things Jitters Drinking a lot of energy drinks Mongo Drinking a lot of beer Rabid Terrorizing humans Slick Being stealthy Speed Racer High-speed driving and crazy car stunts

docs.title: So, How Does This All Work?
docs.text: The core of this game is an improvisational conversation between the player raccoons and the Raccoon Wrangler (RW). The RW describes the raccoons’ current predicament. The players then ask questions and tell the RW what their raccoons do. The RW explains the results of those actions, and the players react again, describing additional actions, and so on.

docs.title: Risky Outcomes
docs.text:
When you do something extraordinary (at least for a raccoon) and inherently risky, with a meaningful outcome, the RW might ask you to roll one six-sided die (d6) to determine the result.

  • If you roll a 5 or 6, you get what you wanted. It's a complete success. You did the thing! Huzzah!
  • If you roll a 4 or less, you still get (mostly) what you wanted, but it’s only a partial success, and an unexpected complication arises.

docs.title: Pushing Your Luck
docs.text:
However, if you want to avoid the complications of a partial success, you can push your luck!

Roll a second d6 and add it to the previous roll.

  • If it's 4 or less, it's still a partial success, no improvement.
  • However, if the total is 5 or 6, it's a complete success! Hooray!

But here's the catch… - If the sum of the two rolls is 7 or higher, it's a complete failure. You don’t get what you want; you probably get what you don’t want, and the RW begins to chortle.

docs.title: What About My Raccoon’s Talent?
docs.text:
When you attempt something risky related to your talent, you can turn a failed result of 7+ into a complete success, once per session. For example, a raccoon with the Mongo talent can ignore a failed beer dice roll and avoid passing out.

Note: The Brains talent is slightly different. It lets you help another raccoon turn a failed result into a success.

Remember, your talent can be used only once per session, so use it wisely.

docs.title: Now with Dumpster Diving!
docs.text:
So, what about starting gear? You don't have any. You're a raccoon.

But you know where to find some: dumpsters!

When you find a dumpster, climb in and start rummaging. Each raccoon rolls d66 twice to make two finds. What’s a d66? Roll a d6 twice, but don’t add the rolls; instead, read the results in order. For example, if you roll a 2 first and then a 4, that’s a 24, and you find a box of toothpicks (lucky you!).

d66 Find d66 Find 11 bag of balloons 41 firecrackers 12 bag of ball bearings 42 flame decal (cool!) 13 baseball bat 43 lighter 14 black leather driving gloves 44 matchbook 15 box of cigars 45 orange safety cone 16 box of expired energy drinks 46 pail of red paint 21 box of expired wine 51 penknife 22 box of nails 52 plush toy raccoon 23 box of surgical masks 53 police siren 24 box of toothpicks 54 roll of dollar bills 25 can of gasoline 55 roll of duct tape 26 car battery 56 rope 31 car jack 61 several feet of chain 32 cassette tape (Queen's Greatest Hits) 62 shopping cart 33 cough syrup 63 spare tire 34 credit card 64 trench coat 35 fake beard and glasses 65 wallet 36 fake ID 66 windshield wipers

Alternatively, use the online BAD ODOR table (Big All-inclusive Digital Online Dumpster Organizational Raster) which includes loads more garbage — even, dare I reveal, a rocket engine.

docs.title: Stress
docs.text:
Face it. You're a raccoon. The world of humans and illegal street racing can be stressful for a small urban critter. Whenever you roll a 7+ (a fail!), you gain one point of stress.

Keep track of your stress level. Events in the story may also add stress, such as sideswiping another car during a race. Your RW will let you know.

docs.title: Stressed-Out
docs.text:
Once your stress level reaches four, you revert to a feral (read: dumb) raccoon. You're out of the action.

Drinking beer is the only way to relax and get back into the action. Each beer removes one point of stress. You're back to your old overachieving self when you're at three or fewer stress points.

See Appendix A for a couple of raccoon-approved cocktail recipes; each concoction removes two points of stress.

docs.title: Inebriation
docs.text: The downside of removing all that stress is drinking all that beer. Keep a running tally of how many beers you’ve consumed. Whenever you drink a beer, roll d6 + beer tally. On a 7+, you pass out and are of little use to anyone. Raccoons are lightweights.

docs.title: Sobering Up
docs.text: How do you sober up and rejoin the adventure? Easy — quaff an energy drink of your choice. An energy drink wakes you up and reduces your beer tally by one point.

docs.title: Totally Wired
docs.text:
Also, keep a running tally of the energy drinks you consume. Whenever you drink one, roll d6 + energy drink tally. On a 7+, you gain a point of stress. Raccoons are lightweights. Oh, wait.

Vicious cycle, huh?

docs.title: What About All These Drinks?
docs.text: You’ll need to find, buy, or swipe some. Rummage a little more through the garbage. Charm a tourist. You’re resourceful. Drinks are out there. Humans seem to love the stuff.

docs.title: How About Car Racing?
docs.text:
First, you’ll have to steal a car. I leave that up to you. Then pop a tape into the cassette player and head out on the open road to your street-racing location.

Once you challenge an opponent, the race begins!

In each round, all raccoons in the car secretly choose one action from the following six racing options — no conferring — and then reveal their choices at the same time.

Picture it. You're scampering around the interior of a car traveling at high speed, frantically working the controls (or drinking beer in the backseat). There's no time to metagame.

Driving Actions

  1. BRAKE
  2. SWERVE RIGHT
  3. SWERVE LEFT
  4. USE AN ITEM FROM YOUR GEAR
  5. ACCELERATE
  6. DO SOMETHING ELSE! (describe it)

The RW resolves your actions in order, one after another, starting with the lowest-numbered action (braking occurs before swerving or accelerating).

Now wake up. It's nighttime, and your smack is ready to race. Find some beer, gear, and a car.

Good luck!

docs.title: Part Two: Raccoon Wrangler
docs.text: So you drew the short straw, eh? Here’s some advice for running a game session.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Everyone at the table, including players and you, the Raccoon Wrangler (RW), should feel safe exploring themes, characters, and storylines that may fall outside everyday conversation. RWs and players should discuss which themes or topics will be in the game, which won’t, and which might appear only briefly.

Everyone at the table must feel comfortable saying “pause” to take a break, “rewind” to revisit a prior situation or decision, and, most importantly, “stop” without fear of judgment if anything in the conversation or game makes them uncomfortable.

If a "stop" is called, remove that scene from the game and steer the narrative toward a different scenario; don't debate its merits.

docs.title: Golden Rules
docs.text:
1. People Matter More Than Games
  2. Fun Matters More Than Rules
  3. Make Player Choices Matter

docs.title: Improvisation
docs.text:
First up, this is all improv. Improvisation is simply making something up on the spot. In role-playing games, improvisation allows RWs to create responses to player actions and events in the game narrative that they didn’t anticipate. If you can think on your feet and devise creative solutions, you can keep the game moving and enjoyable even when things don’t go as you planned.

"As a GM [Raccoon Wrangler] trying to bring actor-style improv to your game, it's your job to say 'yes' whenever a player makes an offer and to encourage the other players to make and accept offers as well."

— Filamena Young, Unframed: The Art of Improvisation for Game Masters (Engine Publishing, 2014).

Never question the whole raccoon thing — play it straight. Run with the hijinks the players dream up, and throw zany encounters and odd situations their way. Make your players make lots and lots of important decisions.

So, when do you roll the dice? As Filamena Young says:

"There will be times when you'll have to say 'no' or otherwise not accept an offer. … In improv theatre, this is called 'blocking,' and it isn't conducive to advancing the story or improving the show. However, you have something that actors don't have! You have dice. As soon as someone blocks an offer, you have a conflict in the game. … Pick up the dice and find out."

Never block your players. If something is risky or uncertain, let the dice decide. Otherwise, just let it happen. “Yes, and” is your tool; never say “no”. Let a dice roll decide “no”, then spin the results back into more hijinks and more decisions.

docs.title: Complications
docs.text:
When players accept a partial success on a die roll, it’s a success for now, but it comes with a tradeoff: complications. It’s now your turn to shine as the RW. Your players are essentially saying, “Bring it on!” The complications you introduce in response to their partially successful actions raise the stakes and add interesting twists to the narrative.

You can always default to adding a point of stress to the raccoons when in doubt, but introducing additional obstacles and circumstances into the narrative is more fun. Consider:

  • Add a new threat — a big dog comes sniffing around.
  • Split the party — clunk, the dumpster lid closed.
  • Use up their gear — ugh, the beer bottles shattered when the car bounced over that speed bump.
  • Give them an ongoing condition — the munchies (they really need to find that food!).

Make your complications fun, odd, and essential. Bring it on!

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
The game session will likely go like this:

  1. The smack wakes up at night in a hollow log, a ditch, or another green spot in a large urban setting, ready for adventure.
  2. Introduce everyone and review their backstories for inspiration. Important: always address your players by their raccoon names.
  3. The smack sets out to find gear and beverages — hijinks.
  4. The smack steals a car — hijinks.
  5. The smack races their rivals — hijinks.

docs.title: Place This in an Actual City
docs.text:
Pick a city you all know. Google Maps Street View is now your friend and battle map.

Find an actual park, riverside area, or wooded section of the city to serve as your adventure's starting point. Then use Street View to identify likely nearby dumpsters and parking lots. Zoom in to spot fancy, racy-looking cars parked in those lots. Find some twisting, isolated stretches of road on Google Maps to stage the race.

Always tie the action and encounters to your actual city and its local flavor and locations. The authenticity of imagining raccoons digging in real dumpsters and driving cars on real roads makes for enjoyable sessions. “Oh yeah, I see a convenience store three blocks over. They have a big orange dumpster on Street View. Let’s head there. And you’ll have to run across a busy highway. But there’s a clump of trees in the median. Wow. Check out that Corvette in the parking lot.”

Set the whole adventure during a Spring Break weekend or at a citywide festival or sporting event. That'll provide plenty of potential beer and inebriated tourists for the smack to interact with.

I guarantee you'll always smile whenever you pass a location from the game in real life.

docs.title: Conducting a Race
docs.text:
The fun of the car race lies in the chaos that erupts when driving actions are revealed simultaneously. The players must never coordinate or collaborate on these moves.

You might randomly determine the opponent’s driving actions or set them manually to maximize chaos and challenge. Throw obstacles in the players’ path and add twists and turns to the racecourse. Go big, go gonzo — jumps, cars ramming each other, a destruction derby, and attackers leaping onto other cars.

Don't play crashes realistically — add a point of stress to all the raccoons in the car, then describe sideswipes, dented fenders, scratched paint, and flying sparks. Introduce a complication or require outcome rolls, but keep the action and the race moving.

Use toy cars and draw a racecourse on paper for in-person play, or load a virtual tabletop with car tokens for an online session. Move the car by its length for each acceleration action. Wing it and make it fun!
